n: The setting is the first year of Darius the Mede, right after Babylon fell to the Persians (about 539–538 BC). A new era had begun, and Daniel wondered what it meant for his people.
Studying the scriptures—Jeremiah’s prophecy—Daniel realized the seventy years of Jerusalem’s desolation were nearly complete. Even a great prophet learns by searching the written word.

f.g: Counted roughly from the first deportation (605 BC) to the return under Cyrus (538 BC).

n: Rather than simply waiting, Daniel turns to God with prayer, fasting, sackcloth, and ashes—signs of humility and mourning.

f.g: Rough goat-hair cloth and ashes, worn as signs of grief and repentance.

n: Daniel’s prayer begins with praise: God is great and awe-inspiring, and keeps His covenant and steadfast love toward those who love and obey Him.
Daniel, though personally righteous, says “we have sinned.” He identifies with his people rather than standing apart from them—a model of intercessory prayer.
Israel ignored the prophets God sent to every level of society—kings, leaders, and ordinary people.

f.w: Neither have we hearkened unto thy servants the prophets

n: God is righteous; Israel deserves the shame they now feel. “Confusion of faces” means open shame. Israel is scattered both near and far.
Shame belongs to every level of the nation—kings, princes, and ancestors—because all sinned.
Yet mercy and forgiveness belong to God. Daniel holds both truths together: our guilt and God’s grace.

f.w: To the Lord our God belong mercies and forgivenesses

n: Israel did not obey the laws God gave through His prophets.
The curses written in the Law of Moses have come upon them because of their disobedience, just as Moses warned.

f.w: the curse is poured upon us

n: God fulfilled His warnings. Nothing anywhere has matched the disaster that struck Jerusalem.

f.w: under the whole heaven hath not been done

n: Even after disaster struck, Israel still did not seek God or turn from sin. Suffering alone doesn’t produce repentance.

f.w: yet made we not our prayer before the LORD

n: God “watched over” the calamity and brought it, because He is just in all He does.

f.g: Kept the threatened disaster ready and carried it out.

n: Daniel appeals to history: the God who rescued Israel from Egypt can rescue them again. Past deliverance is a basis for present hope.

f.w: brought thy people forth out of the land of Egypt

n: He pleads for God to turn His anger from Jerusalem, His holy mountain, which has become a laughingstock to the nations.
“Make your face shine on your desolate sanctuary”—echoing the priestly blessing. Daniel asks for God’s favor to return to the ruined temple.
Daniel asks God to listen and look—not because Israel deserves it, but because of His great mercy. The whole prayer rests on grace.
The prayer climaxes with urgent, short cries: Lord, hear! Lord, forgive! Lord, act! Don’t delay—for the sake of Your own name and people.

f.w: O Lord, hear; O Lord, forgive

n: While Daniel is still praying and confessing—both his own sin and his people’s—the answer comes.
Gabriel, the angel from the earlier vision, arrives swiftly at the time of the evening offering. Though the temple lay in ruins, Daniel still kept its sacred times of prayer.

f.g: The time of the evening sacrifice, about 3 p.m.

n: Gabriel says he has come to give Daniel insight and understanding.
The answer was sent the moment Daniel began praying, because he is “greatly beloved” by God. Heaven responds to sincere prayer immediately, even if the answer takes time to arrive.

f.w: At the beginning of thy supplications

n: “Seventy weeks” (seventy “sevens,” probably 490 years) are decreed for Israel and Jerusalem—to end sin, make atonement, bring everlasting righteousness, fulfill prophecy, and anoint the Most Holy. Christians see these purposes fulfilled through Jesus Christ’s atonement.

f.g: To anoint a most holy place—or, many Christians read, the Most Holy One.

n: From the command to rebuild Jerusalem to the coming of an anointed ruler will be “seven weeks and sixty-two weeks.” Jerusalem will be rebuilt in difficult times—fulfilled in the days of Ezra and Nehemiah.

f.g: Hebrew mashiaḥ nagid—“an anointed one, a ruler.”

f.w: the street shall be built again, and the wall

n: After the sixty-two weeks, “Messiah shall be cut off, but not for himself”—Christians see Christ’s death on behalf of others. A coming ruler’s people will destroy the city and sanctuary, fulfilled when Rome destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70.

f.w: shall Messiah be cut off, but not for himself
shall destroy the city and the sanctuary

n: During the final “week,” a covenant is made, and in the middle of it sacrifices stop. An “abomination of desolation” defiles the temple until the decreed end. Jesus referred to this prophecy in His teachings about Jerusalem’s fall and the last days.

f.g: Often rendered “the abomination that makes desolate.”
